title: Nez Perce Tribe of Indians v. United States
lead: A tribal land-cession claim turned on whether the Commission had mistaken a minimum land value for a maximum and overlooked the scale of the resulting shortfall.

actors.name: Indian Claims Commission
actors.role: Tribunal whose valuation and statutory analysis were reviewed

proceedings: Court of Claims reversed and remanded on unconscionable consideration, while rejecting other grounds and additional interest.
limits: No final compensation award was entered. Valuation discounts were illustrative, and hypothetical lost interest informed unfairness without creating entitlement to interest. Commissioner Scott’s separate view was below, not an appellate concurrence.

review.basis: Individually written and compared with the canonical full brief; no new independent opinion audit claimed.

sections.title: The Tribe cedes the unallotted reservation land
sections.cue: The agreement divides immediate and trust payments
paragraphs: Before the May 1, 1893 agreement, the Nez Perce reservation in northern Idaho contained about 762,000 acres. The agreement provided individual allotments and tribal trust lands, then ceded the remaining 549,559 acres to the United States. Ratification occurred August 15, 1894, the agreed valuation date. The opinion described the price as $2.97 per acre and the total as $1,626,222. Of that, $626,222 was payable per capita as soon as practicable, and $1 million would remain in trust earning 5%.

The ceded land lay principally on a gently rolling plateau east of Lewiston, divided by canyons. Slightly over half suited agriculture, especially cereals, less than a quarter timber, and the remainder grazing. Soils, climate, and regional growth favored development, but access by navigable river, rail, and wagon varied. Allotments tended to retain better agricultural land nearer markets and transport, making simple regional comparisons misleading.

After opening in November 1895, desirable land drew 507 homestead filings in thirteen days. Agricultural acres carried a $3.75 purchase price and stone, timber, and mineral land $5, but much later disposal occurred free under homestead laws. Those prices informed valuation without proving that every acre produced a sale return.

sections.title: The Tribe invokes a special statutory claims remedy
sections.cue: The Commission treats four dollars as a ceiling
paragraphs: Under Indian Claims Commission Act § 2(3) and (5), the Tribe sought revision for fraud, duress, or unconscionable consideration and relief for unfair and dishonorable dealings outside ordinary legal and equitable rules. This was the statutory tribal-claims mechanism, not a private land rescission action.

The Tribe asserted $12.63 per acre, while its appraiser William Brown estimated $11.89. Government appraiser Homer Hoyt estimated $1.29. Both relied mainly on comparable sales with maps, photographs, and soil and transport evidence. Brown used developed land with superior characteristics; Hoyt used fewer, sometimes distant and poorly comparable transactions. The Commission called one optimistic and the other pessimistic, said evidence might support $4 at most, and found the price gap insufficiently unconscionable. It also rejected fraud, duress, and unfair dealings.
Commissioner Scott separately thought the aggregate shortfall unconscionable but believed precedent requiring very gross disparity prevented relief. That was a Commission-stage opinion.

sections.title: The Court of Claims reassesses the evidence’s lower boundary
sections.cue: Illustrative adjustments do not dictate a final appraisal
paragraphs: Judge Laramore agreed with criticisms of both experts but gave greater weight to Brown’s method. Brown’s 20% improvement discount might need to be about 25% to reflect development costs, not merely improvements already present on comparable parcels. Remoteness and access might justify another 20–25%, and the tract’s huge size a similar allowance for subdivision, holding, and resale costs. The Tribe’s constrained bargaining position did not make genuine bulk-development costs imaginary.

Those were exploratory tools, not prescribed discounts on remand. Starting around $20, even aggregate discounts of 65–75% illustrated $5–$7. Seventy-year-old appraisal was inexact, and the court did not know what discounts the Commission used. It also considered the undeveloped acreage and depressed 1894 economy. Nonetheless, substantial evidence supported $4 and the overwhelming weight made it a minimum, not the highest plausible value.

sections.title: Aggregate loss and the minimum value establish unconscionability
sections.cue: The court rejects a mechanical percentage threshold
paragraphs: Precedent required very gross inequality when price alone supplied unconscionability, but no fixed percentage. Earlier cases involving gaps over 100% did not immunize all smaller gaps. The Commission also misused the Miami comparison, whose prior appeal corrected consideration to 38% of value rather than deciding that 63% was adequate.

The $1.03 gap between the stated payment and minimum $4 value, spread over 549,559 acres, was $566,045.77, a substantial 1894 sum. Additional timely consideration likely would have earned trust interest; the court roughly illustrated another $200,000. Most importantly, $4 marked the least a reasonable willing seller would accept, and the legitimate valuation range began there and extended upward. Those combined circumstances met the standard without a mechanical new formula. Neither the differential nor illustrative interest became a money judgment.

sections.title: Economic relevance does not create an interest obligation
sections.cue: The Commission must proceed under the corrected analysis
paragraphs: The Tribe separately sought 5% on added compensation. Although absent from its Commission petition, it said the issue was raised at trial and known thereafter; the court reached entitlement rather than disposing of it for that omission.

Interest against the United States ordinarily required express statutory or contractual authority, apart from the identified constitutional-taking exception. Article III of this agreement fixed the total and made only the specified $1 million remainder interest-bearing. It did not create an open-ended trust for whatever a later court found fair. Pawnee involved an express sum unpaid; this case involved money beyond the promised amount. A likely economic consequence could help show unconscionability without rewriting the interest promise.

On July 15, 1966, the Court of Claims reversed and remanded. Fraud, duress, and unfair and dishonorable dealings remained unproved; unconscionable consideration required further proceedings with $4 treated as a floor. The separate demand for interest failed, and no final compensation amount was set. The report supplies one appellate opinion without a numerical lineup.
